the current word but what the current word implies about upcoming words. The attribution of Left-branching CCG involves forecasting nodes, since Function Composition composes two functions before actually seeing the argument of the second, essentially forecasting such an argument is incoming. Left-CCG is more conservative than left-corner PSG, however, since unary type-changing rules of the CCGbank-style annotation often prevent Function Composition from being applied. The distinction between integration and forecasting nodes will be important for psycholinguistic predictions we make below. Figure 4 illustrates these differences with a sentence from Natural Stories: the integrationcounting variants assign their highest values to phrase-final words, where the syntactically related material has accumulated, whereas the forecasting-counting variants assign high values to phrase-initial words.

2.2 Node Count as an index of structure-building effort

The idea that structure-building operations within the mental parser give rise to cognitive effort dates back to the 1960s (Miller & Chomsky, 1963; Yngve, 1960). Although the specific methods for quantifying such operations differ across studies, the underlying assumption that syntactic structure building imposes processing costs has been widely adopted in research on sentence processing (Frazier, 1985; Hale, 2011; Hawkins, 1994; Kaplan, 1972; Marantz, 2005). Node Count instantiates this perspective by interpreting each node attributed to a word as an operation that the parser performs at that word. Alternatively, some researchers view Node Count as an index of memory load, as structure-building operations should be performed in working memory (Brennan et al., 2016; Shain, Blank, Fedorenko, Gibson, & Schuler, 2022). In either case, the assumption that it reflects processing "difficulty" (Brennan et al., 2012), "complexity" (Bhattasali et al., 2018; Brennan & Pylkkänen, 2017; Brennan et al., 2016; Coopmans et al., 2025; Giglio et al., 2024; Li & Hale, 2019; Stanojević et al., 2023; VanWagenen et al., 2014), or "effort" (Li & Hale, 2019; Lopopolo et al., 2021; Stanojević et al., 2023) is widely accepted. Under this assumption, the processing cost is predicted to correlate positively with Node Count.

Consistent with this prediction, neurolinguistic studies have mostly found positive correlations between Node Count and neural activity. These studies aim to identify when and where syntactic information is processed in the brain by locating regions of interest whose activity positively correlates with Node Count values. For example, several investigations have reported statistically significant positive correlations between Node Count and hemodynamic responses in the left temporal lobe (either anterior or posterior) regions (Brennan et al., 2012 (Brennan et al., , 2016;; Li & Hale, 2019; Stanojević et al., 2023), as well as in the left superior and middle temporal gyri (Giglio et al., 2024; Stanojević et al., 2023). Although several studies have also reported negative correlations (Brennan et al., 2012, p. 170; Stanojević et al., 2023, pp. 23-24; and in production, Giglio et al., 2024, p. 4), the theoretical interpretation of these effects remains an open question. We will return to this point in Section 6.4.

2.3 Node Count as an index of predictability

If Node Count were a proxy for structure-building effort, reading times should correlate positively with it. Contrary to this prediction, behavioral studies examining reading times have found negative effects of Node Count: words with higher Node Count are read faster. Negative effects have been found with dependency-based Node Count in Japanese (Asahara, 2018; Asahara et al., 2019; Isono et al., 2026) and English (Isono, 2024), and CCG-based Node Count in Japanese (Isono et al., 2026).

This pattern can be explained by the effect known as anti-locality (Vasishth & Lewis, 2006), as has been pointed out by Asahara (2018); Asahara et al. (2019); Isono (2024); Isono et al. (2026). Anti-locality effect is called as such because it was originally observed as an effect in verb-final constructions where verbs that complete a longer dependency are easier to process (Konieczny, 2000; Vasishth & Lewis, 2006), contrary to the pattern observed in English relative clauses, for example (Gibson, 1998; Grodner & Gibson, 2005). But it is believed that what is actually responsible for the effect is not the length per se but the expectation for the verb that accumulates as more elements intervene (Konieczny, 2000; Levy, 2008; Vasishth & Lewis, 2006). In fact, Konieczny and Döring (2003) showed in a German reading experiment that changing an intervening element from a postnominal modifier to a preverbal modifier, controlling for length, facilitates the processing of the verb.

Node Count indexes this anti-locality effect, because it counts the number of preceding words that are syntactically related to the current word. Put differently, Node Count reflects the amount of contextual support available for a word during incremental processing. To see why, consider the dependency tree in Figure 5. The Node Count value for problem is two, reflecting the fact that it is dependent on solved and heads a. Both of these words make problem more predictable: solve requires an object to be solved, and problem is a semantically and statistically plausible object of solve; the information from a is less specific but tells that a singular common noun is likely to follow. Compare this with solved, whose Node Count value is one as the only preceding word that is related to it is we. We does inform that a finite verb is going to follow, though it tells little about the lexical identity of the verb. Thus, Node Count based on dependency grammar approximates the amount of contextual information that can contribute to the prediction of an upcoming word.

This connection between Node Count and context richness arises because prior words in a syntactic relation to the target word constrain its possible identity. Syntactic relations inherently entail semantic relations; thus, context words restrict the target word across these dimensions through structural representations. Of course, the amount of contextual information that one syntactic relation provides greatly varies in real texts. Yet, on average, Node Count should correlate with the amount of contextual constraints.

The reasoning above applies to every Node Count that counts integration nodes, and to none that counts forecasting nodes (Section 2.1.4). Each integration node corresponds to a syntactically related element in the preceding context, so the number of such nodes is a proxy for contextual support. The number of forecasting nodes says nothing about how well the current word is supported by its context. We therefore predict that the integrationcounting variants (PSG Bottom-up, Dependency, and CCG-Right) correlate positively with PMI between a word and its context and have facilitatory effects on reading times, whereas the forecasting-counting variants (PSG Top-down and Left-corner) do not. In addition, we expect the facilitatory effect to be stronger for CCG-Right than for CCG-Left, which is partly predictive.

The effort interpretation predicts the opposite pattern: an inhibitory effect for every variant, regardless of the kind of node counted. The result with PSG left-corner will be particularly diagnostic: left-corner parsing has been argued to be cognitively plausible because its memory usage remains minimal for right-and left-branching structures and only grows for center-embedded structures (Abney & Johnson, 1991; Resnik, 1992). A pure structure-building account, therefore, predicts an inhibitory effect of left-corner Node Count. A failure to observe this effect would cast doubt on a straightforward complexity account, although a null result cannot be interpreted as decisive evidence. Table 1 summarizes these predictability-based predictions, along with the effort-based prediction.

We also test whether the effect of Node Count survives when surprisal from a neural large language model (LLM) is controlled for. It is known that the probability of a word that an LLM assigns given the context is strongly predictive of human reading time for that word under the surprisal theory (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008), according to which the

processing cost of a word correlates with the negative logarithm of its probability (Shain et al., 2024; Wilcox, Pimentel, Meister, Cotterell, & Levy, 2023; Xu, Chon, Liu, & Futrell, 2023). Since Node Count is apparently a much coarser metric of predictability, any apparent effect may disappear when LLM surprisal is controlled for. But there is another possibility. Recent work highlights discrepancies between the predictions of LLMs and human reading behavior (Hahn, Futrell, Levy, & Gibson, 2022; Oh & Schuler, 2023; Oh, Yue, & Schuler, 2024). LLM next-word prediction reflects an objective optimized with effectively unbounded contexts and trained on vast amounts of data, which allows the models to achieve far more accurate predictions than humans can make. Given the cognitive resource limitations of humans, humans may rely more on structurally organized context to predict efficiently than LLMs do. In that case, Node Count could retain unique predictive power beyond LLM surprisal.

We conduct two types of analyses. The first analysis looks into the correlation between Node Count and an information-theoretic measure of contextual support (Section 4). The second analysis is a systematic investigation of the relation between Node Count and reading times in English across grammar formalisms, parsing strategies, and datasets, with and without LLM surprisal as a control (Section 5). This design provides the first behavioral test of PSG Node Count, separates integration-counting from forecasting-counting strategies, and compares formalisms under identical criteria.

3 Datasets

We use three large-scale naturalistic reading datasets of English. Dundee (Kennedy & Pynte, 2005) contains eye-tracking data from 10 native speakers reading 20 newspaper articles from The Independent (2,388 sentences; 50,501 words). Natural Stories (Futrell et al., 2021) contains self-paced reading times from 181 native speakers for 10 narrative texts (485 sentences; 10,256 words). OneStop (Berzak et al., 2025) contains eye-tracking data from 180 native speakers reading 10 articles (35,181 words); we use the ordinary-reading portion. For the two eye-tracking datasets, we analyze three standard measures: first-pass duration, go-past duration, and total fixation time (see Rayner, 1998, for a review).

4 Node Count as Context Richness

Our discussion in Section 2.3, like previous behavioral studies, only makes a theoretical argument that Node Count and predictability should be correlated. In this section, we empirically establish this relationship using an information-theoretic measure of context richness, namely, pointwise mutual information (Fano, 1961) between a word and its context (PMI), derived from a large language model. PMI is a measure of statistical association and it has gained growing prominence in psycholinguistics (Futrell, Gibson, & Levy, 2020; Kajikawa, Isono, & Wilcox, 2026; Opedal, Chodroff, Cotterell, & Wilcox, 2024; Wilcox, Pimentel, Meister, & Cotterell, 2024). We test the correlation between PMI and Node Count in three datasets introduced in Section 3.

4.1 Information-theoretic measure of context richness

PMI between a word and its context is defined as follows: where P(•) denotes the probability of a linguistic unit, w i is the word at position i and w <i is its preceding words, and surp(•) := -log 2 P(•) denotes surprisal (information content).

PMI between w i and w <i quantifies the amount of information about w i provided by conditioning on w <i . Intuitively, it measures the strength of contextual support for w i . This measure of context richness conceptually aligns with Node Count. To recap, we hypothesize that the integration-counting Node Count variants (Section 2.1.4)-PSG Bottomup, Dependency, and, in practice, both CCG variants-reflect the number of syntactically and therefore semantically relevant prior words and thus serve as proxies for the contextual support. Since these context words contribute to constraining the plausible candidates for the upcoming word, a higher Node Count implies greater contextual support. What Node Count is meant to capture is the contribution of context words w <i , not the overall predictability of the target word w i . The information-theoretic counterpart should, therefore, isolate the contribution of w <i as well. Conditional surprisal surp(w i | w <i ) does not, although widely used as a measure of word (un)predictability (Levy, 2008; Smith & Levy, 2013), as it conflates how predictable w i is without context and how much w <i contributes. PMI quantifies how much the information of w <i improves the predictability of w i (see Equations ( 1) to ( 4)). We therefore take PMI, rather than conditional surprisal, as the information-theoretic counterpart of Node Count.

We estimate PMI as the difference between the estimated unigram surprisal of w i and the estimated conditional surprisal of w i given w <i . The use of corpus-based estimation of word probabilities represents the assumption that probabilities derived from a large-scale corpus serve as a robust statistical proxy for human subjective expectations during online sentence comprehension (Shain et al., 2024; Smith & Levy, 2013). Unigram surprisals are estimated from approximately 33 billion pre-tokenized tokens of the Pile dataset (Gao et al., 2020) using the code by Oh et al. (2024). We use the 124M-parameter GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) foot_1 to estimate word-by-word conditional surprisal. The choice of the parameter size is matched with the reading time analysis, where this size is chosen based on previous studies that report a better fit with smaller parameters (see Section 5.2). For this estimation, we apply whitespace-trailing decoding (Oh & Schuler, 2024), a method that reallocates the probability of a leading whitespace token to the preceding word. Conditional surprisals are computed using at most the preceding 1,023 tokens as context due to this decoding method (the maximum 1,024 context window supported by GPT-2 minus one token for estimating the probability of the following whitespace).

4.2 Computing Node Count

We compute Node Count values under the three grammar formalisms described in Section 2.1 for each of the three datasets. Where available, we use gold-standard parses: For Dundee, we use UD-style gold annotations (Barrett, Agić, & Søgaard, 2015); for Natural Stories, we employ both UD-style and Penn Treebank-style parses (Futrell et al., 2021). Where gold-standard parses are unavailable, we use silver-standard parses generated by neural parsers. Penn Treebank-style constituency parses are obtained using the Berkeley Neural Parser (benepar) (Kitaev, Cao, & Klein, 2019; Kitaev & Klein, 2018). 3 Dependency parses are produced using Stanza (Qi, Zhang, Zhang, Bolton, & Manning, 2020),foot_3 and CCG parses are produced using ccgtools (Stanojević & Steedman, 2019). Since ccgtools generates right-branching structures reflecting the original treebank (Hockenmaier & Steedman, 2007), we transformed the generated parses into the maximally incremental ones by rotating entire structures to the left as much as possible. Note that this does not mean that the resulting structures are fully left-branching, as fully incremental parsing is not only theoretically impossible for certain constructions (such as English object relative clauses) (Demberg, 2012), but is also practically hindered by the unary type-changing rules inherent in the CCGbank-style annotation.

Before turning to the statistical analyses, we report the distributions of Node Count values to make their magnitudes and typical ranges transparent to the reader. As shown in Figure 6, the distributions of Node Count values are highly skewed toward lower values across all formalisms. In predictive parsing variants such as top-down and left-corner, the most frequently observed value is 1. CCG-Left also peaks at 1, as its left-branching derivations permit eager composition; however, compared with the PSG left-corner, it contains more words with 0, suggesting that fully left-branching derivations are not always achieved. 5Thus, whenever local integration is supported at early stages of processing, the mode is 1, whereas it is 0 in other formalisms.

4.3 Correlation between Node Count and PMI

We calculate correlations between Node Count variants and PMI. To mitigate sensitivity to extreme values, we report both Pearson's (r) and Spearman's rank correlation (ρ).

The results are shown in Figure 7. Consistent with the predictions in Table 1, PSG Bottom-up, Dependency, and CCG variants show stable positive correlations, whereas PSG Top-down and Left-corner show weak or negative correlations. This supports the view that Node Count is correlated with the amount of lexical, syntactic, or semantic constraints and is thus highly related to context richness. The Pearson correlation coefficients among Node Counts, word positions, word length, unigram surprisal, GPT-2 surprisal, and PMI are also reported in Figure A.2 in Appendix A. While word length and unigram surprisal show positive correlations (around 0.2 to 0.3) with the Node Counts for PSG Bottom-up, Dependency, and CCG, the other variables show little to no correlation in most cases. 5 Analyzing Naturalistic Reading Time

5.1 Reading-time measures and preprocessing

For the two eye-tracking datasets (Dundee and OneStop), we examine three standard eyetracking measures. (i) First pass duration (also referred to as gaze duration): the total time spent between the gaze's first entry into the region and the first exit in either direction. This measure is thought to reflect lexical access and early syntactic and semantic processing. (ii) Go-past duration (also known as regression path duration): the total time spent between the gaze's first entry into the region and the first exit to the right. (iii) Total fixation time: the total time spent in that region, including regressions. This reflects overall processing difficulty, including reanalysis. For further discussion of these measures, see Rayner (1998).

Prior to statistical analysis, we apply the following preprocessing steps. We exclude the first and last words of each sentence, as well as words that contain punctuation, to eliminate sentence-boundary and punctuation-related effects, such as wrap-up effects (Demberg & Keller, 2008) and implicit prosody (Breen, 2014). In the Dundee and OneStop data, we remove data points with durations of 0 ms or above 2,000 ms. For OneStop, we additionally exclude trials presented during the practice phase. For Natural Stories, we follow the authors (Futrell et al., 2021) and exclude reading times shorter than 100 ms or longer than 3,000 ms, as well as responses from participants who answered fewer than 5 out of 6 comprehension questions correctly for a given story.

All reading times are averaged across participants to control for individual variability, as in previous work (Smith & Levy, 2013; Wilcox et al., 2023). We analyze raw reading time rather than applying a non-linear transformation such as a log transformation, as previous work has robustly established that the effect of surprisal, a key control variable in our analysis, exhibits a linear relationship with raw reading time (Shain et al., 2024; Smith & Levy, 2013; Wilcox et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023). After preprocessing, the resulting dataset includes 37,263 data points from Dundee, 8,579 from Natural Stories, and 29,606 from OneStop. The distributions of reading times analyzed are reported in Figure A.1 in Appendix A.

5.2 Statistical analysis

Our statistical analyses address the three questions introduced in Section 1: (i) which Node Count variants predict reading times, and in which direction; (ii) whether their contributions are non-redundant across formalisms; and (iii) whether they survive controlling for surprisal from a Transformer-based language model.

To answer question (i), we follow prior studies (Fossum & Levy, 2012; Frank & Bod, 2011; Goodkind & Bicknell, 2018; Wilcox et al., 2023) and assess whether the inclusion of Node Count into the regression model improves reading time prediction. Specifically, we compare a baseline regression model without Node Count against a target model that includes it, and evaluate whether the target model achieves significantly higher log-likelihood on held-out test data.

More precisely, the dataset D used for statistical analysis is denoted as: where y i is the mean reading time for word w i , x i is a vector of explanatory variables derived from w i , and N is the total number of observations.

We fit a linear regression model of the form: where β 0 represents the intercept and β is the vector of coefficients.

N (0, σ 2 ) denotes a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a variance of σ 2 . We compare the following two models. The baseline model includes lexical and positional predictors that are known to influence reading time. These predictors are word position in the whole article (zone), word position in the sentence (position), orthographic word length (wlen), unigram surprisal (unisurp), and the interaction of wlen and unisurp, as well as the spillover effects of wlen, unisurp and their interaction from the previous region. We use the unigram surprisal estimates described in Section 4.1.

The target model extends the baseline model by adding Node Counts from the current and previous two words:

A note on indexing: because the model for y i contains the Node Counts of the current and two preceding words, the coefficient of NC i-1 captures the effect of a word's Node Count on the reading time of the following word. Throughout, we describe effects by the region in which they surface: an effect at w i+1 refers to the coefficient of NC i-1 , and at w i+2 to that of NC i-2 ; figure axes follow the same convention.

The predictive utility of Node Count is evaluated using k-fold cross-validation, where k = 10 (10-fold CV). The dataset is randomly partitioned into ten equally sized folds. For each fold, the models are trained on the remaining nine folds and evaluated on the held-out fold. For every test-set observation i, we calculate the word-wise difference in log-likelihood (∆ (i) LL ) between the target and baseline models: where p(y | x, β 0 , β, σ 2 ) is the probability density function of the normal distribution corresponding to the regression model in Equation ( 6).

The parameters β0 , β, and σ2 represent the intercept, coefficient vector, and variance, respectively, estimated from the training folds for each model. Log-likelihoods are computed with the natural logarithm. ∆ LL is thus reported in nats. We test whether the mean of the word-by-word ∆ (i) LL , or ∆ LL for short, is greater than zero using a permutation test (a one-sided sign-flipping randomization test) with 20, 000 iterations. The significance threshold for each test is corrected for multiple comparisons across datasets using the Benjamini-Hochberg method (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), with a target of α = 0.05.

In parallel, we examine the estimated regression coefficients β for Node Counts to assess their direction. The relationships between residual reading times from the baseline model and Node Count are reported in Figure A.3 in Appendix A.

For question (ii), we perform model selection based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974). For each dataset, let n be the number of Node Count variants that significantly improved fit in (i). We treat each variant's three regional terms (NC i , NC i-1 , NC i-2 ; effects at w i , w i+1 , w i+2 ) as a block that enters or leaves the model together, fit all 2 n models on a random half of the data, and select the model with the lowest AIC. We then refit the selected model on the held-out half and test each regional coefficient against zero with a two-sided t test (α = 0.05).

To address question (iii), we repeat the 10-fold CV regression analysis, augmenting the baseline model with surprisal estimated from a Transformer-based language model. We estimate word-by-word surprisal using the smallest (124M parameters) version of GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), since this model has been shown to outperform larger models in predicting reading times (Oh & Schuler, 2023; Shain et al., 2024). We test whether Node Count continues to explain a variance in reading times above and beyond what is accounted for by GPT-2 surprisal. Since our baseline already includes unigram surprisal, adding GPT-2 surprisal is mathematically equivalent to controlling for contextual PMI (Opedal et al., 2024) examined in Section 4.

All predictors used in our statistical analyses are z-transformed. The Pearson correlation coefficients of the predictors are reported in Figure In the remainder of this section, we address questions (i)-(iii) in turn, evaluating the predictive power and direction of Node Count (Section 5.3), its independence across grammar formalisms (Section 5.5), and its relationship to Transformer-based surprisal (Section 5.6).

5.3 Predictive power and direction of Node Count

As expected, we find that PSG Bottom-up, Dependency, and CCG-Right consistently show significant predictive power for reading times, with a negative coefficient in the immediate regions.

Figure 8 shows the mean ∆ log-likelihoods across words (∆ LL ) with 95% confidence intervals. The predictive power of Node Count varies systematically depending on the grammar formalism and strategy in a manner consistent with the predictions in Table 1. Specifically, variants that primarily track the amount of context, namely PSG Bottom-up, Dependency, and CCG-Right, showed consistent effects, significant in all seven tests. By contrast, variants involving forecasting nodes exhibited weaker predictive power, as anticipated. CCG-Left and PSG Top-down showed significant effects in six out of seven tests. PSG Left-corner improved model fit only in the OneStop Go-past condition. Additionally, CCG-Left tends to yield weaker predictive power than CCG-Right.

Figure 9 shows the mean regression coefficients for each Node Count (both main and spillover regions), estimated over the 10-fold CV.

Overall, PSG Bottom-up, PSG Left-corner, Dependency, CCG-Right, and CCG-Left tend to show consistent negative effects across datasets in the w i and w i+1 regions, while PSG Top-down does not. This is consistent with the view that Node Count reflects the predictability of the current word due to the structured context. On the other hand, PSG Bottom-up and CCG show strong positive effects in the w i+2 region across all datasets except * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * Dundee First pass Dundee Go-past Dundee Total fixation Natural Stories OneStop First pass OneStop Go-past OneStop Total fixation 0.000 0.002 0.004 0.006 0.008 Delta Log Likelihood (average per word) PSG Top-down PSG Bottom-up PSG Left-corner Dependency CCG-Right CCG-Left for OneStop Go-past, which is contrary to the expectations from the view that Node Count indexes predictability.

We discuss this issue in the follow-up analysis in the next Section 5.4.

5.4 Investigating the sign reversal

Below, we examine why the effect of Node Count flips signs in the spillover regions.

To avoid artifacts that might arise from shared variance among Node Count across regions r ∈ {i, i -1, i -2}, we fit separate regression models for each region r that add NC r as the sole Node Count term to the baseline model (introduced in Section 5.2) and evaluate its predictive power and coefficient using 10-fold CV.

The results are shown in Figure 10. The Node Count variants that showed a positive coefficient in later regions in the previous analysis mostly remain significant with a positive coefficient: PSG Bottom-up and CCG-Right were significantly positive at w i+2 in 6 out of 7 datasets, and CCG-Left was significantly positive in 5 out of 7 datasets. This indicates that the observed late slowdowns in Figure 9 are unlikely to be a statistical artifact of shared variance across regions, but instead reflect a systematic inhibitory effect captured by Node Count.

What caused the sign reversal from negative to positive? A slowdown that follows a speedup is either (a) a mere backlash of that speedup, with no processing cost of its own, or (b) a genuine cost; and a genuine cost is either (b-i) syntactic, the cost of building syntactic structure, or (b-ii) non-syntactic, the cost of integrating the word with its context at the semantic or discourse level. We consider these possibilities in turn.

The backlash hypothesis (a) says that when the reader encounters a predictable word, they move on to the next word immediately, but that can sometimes be too fast-if predictability is not the sole factor affecting processing difficulty (contra Levy, 2008), the subsequent processing of the predictable word can be the bottleneck, resulting in a slowdown in later regions. If this explanation is on the right track, the pattern should not be specific to Node Count. A similar cross-regional sign reversal should also be observable for any metric of predictability, including surprisal (Demberg & Keller, 2008; Shain et al., 2024; Smith & Levy, 2013; Wilcox et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023). To test this prediction, we add GPT-2 surprisal at w i and its spillover to the baseline regression model described in Section 5.2 and examine its coefficients averaged over the 10-fold CV. Since surprisal quantifies how unpredictable a word is given its context (negative predictability), compensatory patterns would predict positive effects at w i and w i+1 but a sign flip to a negative effect at w i+2 in our datasets. The result in Figure 11 shows that across all datasets, surprisal exhibited positive effects in every region, including w i+2 . Thus, we find no evidence of compensatory sign reversal for surprisal. The remaining accounts, (b-i) structure building cost and (b-ii) non-syntactic integration cost, can be separated empirically. On the syntactic account (b-i), the late slowdown is the cost of structure building. If so, the slowdown should be at least as robust for a variant whose attribution rule follows a cognitively plausible parsing strategy, and left-corner parsing is such a strategy: it keeps memory demands manageable in both left-and right-branching configurations (Abney & Johnson, 1991; Resnik, 1992). But PSG Left-corner Node Count improved fit only in the OneStop Go-past measure, with a negative coefficient (Figures 8 to 10). On the non-syntactic account (b-ii), the late slowdown is the cost of a post-syntactic integrative process, for example, establishing the semantic relations between the word and the representation built so far, once sufficient structure is available. This account predicts the observed contrast: the cost should scale with the amount of contextual material relevant to the word, which PSG Bottom-up and CCG track and PSG Left-corner does not (Section 4). It does so regardless of the parser's structural backbone: even if the backbone is left-corner, the post-syntactic process still has to integrate the word with the constraints its context supplies.

We therefore take account (b-ii) to be the most plausible interpretation of the delayed

5.5 Best model selection

We then examined whether the effects of different Node Count variants were independent of each other by best model selection described in detail in Section 5.2. Figure 12 shows the results of this analysis. The results vary across datasets and word positions, but the overall trend is that Dependency is the most likely to remain (6 out of 7 datasets). The next most frequent co-occurring variants are PSG Bottom-up and CCG-Right (retained in 4 out of 7 datasets), whereas PSG Top-down, Left-corner, and CCG-Left are rarely or never retained. The results indicate that Node Counts derived from different grammar formalisms, specifically when they capture context richness, can explain non-redundant variance in reading time.

The signs of the retained coefficients largely reproduce the dual nature of Node Count found in the previous analyses: negative in the immediate regions, positive in the late region for the constituency-based variants, with CCG-Right in Natural Stories as the one exception. Dependency was negative wherever it was retained, and PSG Bottom-up was negative at w i and w i+1 in every dataset in which it was retained. The positive coefficients were those of PSG Bottom-up at w i+2 in Dundee Go-past, CCG-Left at w i+2 in Dundee First-pass, and CCG-Right at w i+1 and w i+2 , as well as at w i in Natural Stories.

Two further observations concern which variants are retained together. First, the negative effects of Dependency and PSG Bottom-up survive each other's inclusion, so the predictability they index is not the same: the two variants pick out contextual support at different

Dundee First pass Dundee Go-past Dundee Total fixation Natural Stories OneStop First pass OneStop Go-past OneStop Total fixation structural boundaries, a point we develop in Section 6.2. Second, PSG Bottom-up and CCG-Right, the two variants with the most robust late slowdowns, were never retained together at spillover regions. This is what one expects if their late effects are not independently detectable as distinct components, likely reflecting the shared contextual semantic integration proposed in Section 5.4.

5.6 Controlling Transformer-based language model surprisal

To determine whether the effect of Node Count persists beyond what can be explained by modern predictability measures, we added GPT-2 surprisal of the main and two spillover regions to our baseline regression model and examined the resulting ∆ LL . Figure 13 shows ∆ LL with 95% confidence intervals. In this figure, predictors that were previously significant (as reported in Section 5.3) are shown again, with the results after controlling for GPT-2 surprisal indicated using open circles. Adding GPT-2 surprisal to the baseline regression model reduced the ∆ LL of Node Count in 29 out of 33 variant-dataset combinations; the four exceptions were PSG Top-down in the Dundee and OneStop Go-past measures and PSG Bottom-up and CCG-Right in Natural Stories. Despite the reduction, 29 out of 33 combinations remained statistically significant after the control. These results suggest two things. First, Node Count and GPT-2 surprisal account for an overlapping portion of variance in reading times. This is consistent with the view that the behavioral effect of Node Count is due to its correlation with predictability. Second, Node Count still captures aspects of human reading that are not captured by GPT-2. This is possibly because human sentence comprehension relies more on structured contexts than GPT-2 does to cope with memory limitations.

6 General Discussion

This study examined whether syntactic Node Count, a linking hypothesis widely used in neurolinguistic research as an index of structure-building effort, instead indexes structuremediated predictability. Using three large-scale naturalistic datasets of reading times in English, we found that the integration-counting variants (PSG Bottom-up, Dependency, and CCG) correlate positively with PMI between a word and its context and speed up reading in the immediate regions, and that the constituency-based variants among them also slow reading down in spillover regions. We also found that Node Counts based on different formalisms explained non-redundant variance, and the effects persisted after controlling for GPT-2 surprisal. Below, we discuss what these results say about Node Count itself (Section 6.1), about the representations humans use for prediction (Sections 6.2 and 6.3), and about the neurolinguistic uses of Node Count (Section 6.4).

6.1 Node Count quantifies the amount of contextual information

The immediate negative effect of Node Count should be interpreted as a predictability effect. The direction of the effect is what expectation-based accounts predict (Hale, 2001 (Hale, , 2016;; Levy, 2008): a word that stands in more syntactic relations to the preceding context is more strongly constrained by that context, hence more predictable, and the integration-counting variants accordingly speed up reading at w i and w i+1 . The result in Section 4 supports this * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * Dundee First pass Dundee Go-past Dundee Total fixation Natural Stories OneStop First pass OneStop Go-past OneStop Total fixation 0.000 0.003 0.006 0.009 Delta Log Likelihood (average per word) PSG Top-down PSG Bottom-up PSG Left-corner Dependency CCG-Right CCG-Left w/o surprisal w/ surprisal interpretation: the variants that speed up reading are exactly those that correlate positively with PMI between a word and its context, which measures contextual support.

Two further contrasts between variants argue against a structure-building interpretation on which this facilitation would be incidental. The effect is absent for PSG Left-corner, the cognitively plausible parsing strategy among PSG parsing strategies, and within CCG the right-branching variant predicts reading times better than the left-branching one, as expected if what matters is how closely the count tracks accumulated context (Section 2.1.4) rather than how incremental the derivation is. The results thus extend the negative effects of dependency-and CCG-based Node Count reported earlier (Asahara, 2018; Asahara et al., 2019; Isono, 2024; Isono et al., 2026) to phrase-structure-based Node Count, the variant most used in neurolinguistic work, and support the interpretation those studies proposed.

By contrast, we interpret the late positive effect as a cost, but not a syntactic one. As discussed in Section 5.4, it is not a mere backlash of the earlier speedup. Nor does it seem to be the cost of structure building. We therefore read it as the cost of a post-syntactic process that integrates the word with the contextual elements it is related to. This is not to deny that structure building has a cost. Such a cost may well be correlated with Node Count, but in reading times it does not appear as an immediate slowdown, presumably because the predictability effect masks it. Other proposed metrics may be more promising to capture this cost (e.g., Demberg, Keller, & Koller, 2013; Gibson, 2000; Hale, 2011; Hale, Dyer, Kuncoro, & Brennan, 2018; Isono, 2024; Kobele, Gerth, & Hale, 2013; Reddy & Wehbe, 2021). What the results show is that Node Count cannot be used as a metric of structure-building cost without taking into account both its predictability component and its delayed integration component, a point with consequences for the neurolinguistic uses of Node Count that we develop in Section 6.4.

One pattern the predictability account does not explain is the residual predictive power of PSG Top-down Node Count, which improved model fit in six of seven tests (Figure 8) despite correlating negatively with PMI (Figure 7) and showing no consistent direction across regions (Figure 9). If anything, its negative PMI correlation would predict inhibitory effects under the predictability account, while a structure-building account predicts consistently positive effects; neither pattern holds. We leave the interpretation of this variant open.

Although our reading-time evidence is limited to English, a head-initial language, the predictability interpretation is consistent with what has been found in head-final languages. Context richness should matter in these languages because pre-verbal arguments strongly constrain the prediction of the clause-final verb, which is the configuration in which antilocality effects were first observed (Konieczny, 2000; Konieczny & Döring, 2003; Levy, 2008; Vasishth & Lewis, 2006). Consistent with this, studies of Japanese have found negative correlations between reading times and Node Count derived from dependency and CCG parses (Asahara, 2018; Asahara et al., 2019; Isono & Kajikawa, 2026; Isono et al., 2026).

Finally, the two studies that report a positive immediate effect of CCG-based Node Count in English (Kajikawa et al., 2024; Ozaki et al., 2024) are not in conflict with our results, because they count something different. Those studies included Type Raising and type-changing rules in their count. As noted in Section 2.1, the former is regarded as a morpho-lexical operation, and the latter lacks a clear theoretical justification. Also, neither records a relation between the current word and its context. When Node Count is restricted to binary combinatory rules, as here, it shows the negative immediate effect and the delayed positive effect that the contextual interpretation predicts.

6.2 Evidence for concurrent tracking of multiple structural dimensions

Our best model selection analysis revealed that Node Counts derived from different grammar formalisms often explained unique variance in reading times. Specifically, the best models often contained Node Counts from both a constituency-based grammar (PSG Bottom-up or CCG) and Dependency. Different formalisms organize the context in different ways. That Node Counts based on different formalisms explain non-redundant variance suggests that each of these formalisms captures some aspects of the actual representation that humans use to compress contextual information and predict the upcoming word. One possibility is that these formalisms reflect different levels of analysis that are concurrently tracked in the human mind (Christiansen & Chater, 2016; Jackendoff, 2023; Lopopolo et al., 2021). Both Constituency-and Dependency-based Node Count capture lexical, syntactic, and semantic constraints, but they correlate with these constraints based on different structural boundaries: Constituency-based Node Count tracks the completion of phrases, while Dependency Node Count captures direct relations between words: for example, the Node Count values for the sentence We solved a problem analytically are [1, 0, 0, 2, 3] under PSG Bottomup and [0, 1, 0, 2, 1] under Dependency. The former yields non-zero values strictly at phrase boundaries, scaling with the size of the completed constituent, whereas the latter registers them as each dependency is resolved, even mid-phrase. Consequently, these metrics capture qualitatively distinct predictability effects.

The same logic naturally extends from prediction to integration. As discussed in Sec-tion 5.4, the late slowdowns captured by some Node Counts likely reflect the cost of semantic integration. These delayed costs are prominent for Constituency-based Node Counts but absent for Dependency (see Figures 9, 10 and 12). We speculate that this asymmetry arises because Constituency-based Node Counts track the completion of phrases, where the effect of semantic integration is concentrated, akin to a wrap-up effect, whereas Dependency does not. Importantly, Node Count cannot tell us which parsing strategy is cognitively plausible. The correlation between integration-counting Node Count and the amount of contextual constraint is independent of the parser's strategy, unless one adopts the unrealistic assumption that the predictive mechanism has no access other than to the active nodes in the tree. Accordingly, despite the current results showing bottom-up Node Count variants fare better in predicting reading time than left-corner and top-down variants, we do not claim that the human parser constructs structures in a bottom-up manner. Still, the current results suggest that the context humans use for prediction is organized by syntactic structures.

6.3 Prediction based on structural representation beyond statistical patterns

The explanatory power of Node Count persisted even after controlling for surprisal from GPT-2, a powerful statistical language model. This means that a simple, linguistically motivated structural metric captures aspects of predictability in human sentence processing that are not fully subsumed by the rich co-occurrence statistics learned by Transformers.

While modern language models generate next-word probabilities using distributed representations learned from large-scale text, humans may rely on more resource-rational computations under cognitive constraints such as limited working memory (Hahn et al., 2022; Isono & Kajikawa, 2026; Lieder & Griffiths, 2020; Xu & Futrell, 2026). In particular, comprehenders may selectively maintain and prioritize structurally relevant information in memory and use explicit linguistic structure to guide prediction. From this perspective, Node Count may index structure-mediated predictability, reflecting the extent to which prediction is supported by such structure-based, resource-efficient representations. One reason GPT-2 surprisal does not subsume Node Count in predicting human reading time may be that the Transformers' mechanisms for weighting contextual information are not biased toward structure-relevant cues. Consistent with this possibility, Transformers that incorporate explicit syntactic structure via syntax-constrained attention masks (Sartran et al., 2022) have been shown to predict human reading times better than standard token-based Transformers (Yoshida et al., 2025).

Our results highlight not only a potential architectural difference between large language models and human cognition, but also underscore the importance of employing representationspecific metrics. Unlike representation-agnostic information-theoretic measures such as surprisal, metrics grounded in specific linguistic theories provide more constrained hypotheses about the actual representations driving human language processing (Isono, 2024; Slaats & Martin, 2025; Stanojević et al., 2023).

6.4 Implications for neurolinguistic uses of Node Count

The dual profile of Node Count suggests a specific reading of the mixed neural findings reviewed in Section 2.2. Hemodynamic responses integrate over several seconds, so an fMRI regressor built from Node Count conflates two temporally distinct components. The first is an immediate reduced activation due to greater structure-mediated predictability. Previous studies show that less surprising words elicit reduced N400 (Frank, Otten, Galli, & Vigliocco, 2015; Kutas & Federmeier, 2011) and less activity in naturalistic fMRI, MEG, and EEG (Heilbron, Armeni, Schoffelen, Hagoort, & de Lange, 2022; Shain, Blank, van Schijndel, Schuler, & Fedorenko, 2020; Willems, Frank, Nijhof, Hagoort, & van den Bosch, 2016). The second is a delayed integration cost. Which component dominates the measured correlation can then vary with region, task, and model specification, producing positive correlations in some studies and negative ones in others (e.g., Brennan et al., 2012; Giglio et al., 2024; Stanojević et al., 2023). This account yields a testable prediction. In time-resolved measures such as MEG and EEG, Node Count from integration-counting variants should show a biphasic response: an early component consistent with facilitation, followed by a later component consistent with integration cost. A forecasting-counting variant such as PSG Left-corner should show neither. Existing MEG findings linking Node Count to delta-band activity (Coopmans et al., 2025; Slaats et al., 2024) provide a natural starting point for testing this decomposition.

6.5 Limitations

We acknowledge several limitations. First, like all work using Node Count, our analyses assume a "perfect oracle" parser (Brennan, 2016). Node Count values presuppose the globally correct parse, whereas real-time comprehension faces local ambiguity. This idealization is arguably less problematic for the predictability interpretation: context words that will turn out to be related to w i constrain its identity whether or not the parser has committed to the correct analysis. Even so, the mapping from oracle counts to online expectations remains an approximation. Second, gold parses were available for only part of the data; elsewhere we relied on silver parses, whose errors add noise to Node Count. Third, our reading-time evidence is limited to English. We outline predictions for head-final languages above, which are consistent with observations from previous studies in Japanese (Asahara, 2018; Asahara et al., 2019; Isono et al., 2026), but do not test them here. Fourth, our regressions are fit to participant-averaged reading times, which follows standard practice in the computational psycholinguistic literature (Smith & Levy, 2013; Wilcox et al., 2023) but leaves participantlevel variability unmodeled. Finally, our language-model control is a single model, GPT-2 (124M). Although it provides the best reading-time fit among Transformer LMs reported to date, our conclusion that Node Count captures variance beyond LLM surprisal is, strictly, a conclusion about this model.

7 Conclusion

This study provides evidence from large-scale, naturalistic reading data that syntactic Node Count primarily indexes context richness, yielding robust facilitation through prediction and a delayed slowdown most consistent with contextual semantic integration. Our findings also suggest that humans employ multiple streams of structural analysis and leverage them for predictive processing in ways that are not fully captured by surprisal from GPT-2, the Transformer language model with the best reported fit to human reading times. This work points to the need for a careful interpretation of how Node Count functions as a linking hypothesis in psycholinguistics and neurolinguistics and highlights the critical role of syntactic structure in the mechanisms of human predictive processing.

A Descriptive statistics and model diagnostics

B Bayesian mixed-effects analysis of PMI and Node Count

This appendix verifies that the correlations in Figure 7 in Section 4 reflect a genuine association between Node Count and contextual support, rather than just target-word frequency.

Data We analyze the Natural Stories corpus as a representative case; the raw Node Count-PMI correlations are of comparable magnitude across the three datasets (Figure 7), so we do not expect the conclusions to depend on this choice. We exclude words attached to punctuation and words at line boundaries, as in the reading time analyses. Each word is assigned a Universal Dependencies-style POS tag (de Marneffe et al., 2021) using Stanza (Qi et al., 2020); when a whitespace-delimited word spans several tokens (e.g., clitics), the tags are concatenated. POS categories with fewer than 50 tokens are excluded. This leaves 8,466 words across 13 POS categories in Natural Stories. The two covariates address two potential confounds. First, by Equations ( 1) to ( 4), PMI is mechanically larger for low-frequency words, for which context has more room to reduce uncertainty. Second, word categories differ in both mean PMI and mean Node Count. Content words, for example, tend to have higher unigram surprisal. The by-POS random effects absorb such category-level covariation, so the fixed coefficient estimates the typical within-category association. Since Node Count is centered and PMI is left on its natural scale, the coefficient reads as bits of PMI per additional node count.

Model

Priors and inference

We use weakly informative priors on the bit scale: N (0, 10) for the intercept, N (0, 2) for the fixed-effect coefficients, half-N (0, 2) for random-effect standard deviations, LKJ(2) for their correlations, and an exponential prior with rate 0.25 for the residual standard deviation. Models were fit using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2025). Sampling was executed with CmdStanR (Gabry, Češnovar, Johnson, & Bronder, 2025) using 4 chains of 2,000 iterations, including 1,000 warmup draws. All ˆ︁ R values were less than 1.01. Prior sensitivity analysis To ensure that our results are not overly dependent on the specific choices of priors, we conducted a sensitivity analysis. We varied the standard deviations (SDs) of the fixed-effect coefficient priors across 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10 (we used SD=2 above). As shown in Figure B.2, while extremely restrictive priors (e.g., SD = 0.1) shrank the estimates toward zero and caused the 95% credible intervals to include zero, the direction of the effects (posterior medians) remained consistent across all prior specifications, indicating that our main conclusions are robust to the choice of priors.

These studies report a positive correlation between combinatory categorial grammar (CCG) Node Count and reading time. As discussed in Section 6.1, their results are probably a consequence of including unary CCG operations in that count, which may be lexical rather than syntactic in nature.

One might expect structure-based language models, such as probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFG;Jelinek & Lafferty, 1991; Stolcke, 1995), Recurrent Neural Network Grammars(Dyer, Kuncoro, Ballesteros, & Smith, 2016), or Transformer Grammars(Sartran et al., 2022), to be better suited for estimating conditional surprisal in this context, given that Node Count is derived from syntactic parses. However, this is not the case. This is because the context richness reflected by Node Count is not restricted to syntactic constraints but encompasses broader lexico-semantic and higher-level linguistic dimensions. Nevertheless, if our assumption holds, one might expect the PMI estimated via lexicalized PCFGs(Charniak, 1997; Collins, 2003) to exhibit a higher correlation with Node Count than that estimated from unlexicalized PCFGs. Since lexicalized PCFGs suffer from severe data sparsity when applied to naturalistic text, complicating the stable estimation of PMI, we leave this empirical comparison for future research.

Since the neural constituency parser for PSG does not output phonologically null elements such as traces of "movement" or "ellipsis", we remove such elements from the gold constituency parses in Natural Stories to maintain consistency across corpora.

As for dependency node count, we exclude the "root" and "punct" relations.

In CCG, fully left-branching derivations correspond to maximally incremental parsing. As such derivations apply exactly one binary combinatory rule at each non-initial word, they would assign NC= 1 to all non-initial words shown in Figure

The fact that the empirical distribution contains substantial mass at NC= 0 therefore indicates clear departures from full incrementality.

As shown in Equations (1) to (4), PMI is mechanically larger for low-frequency words. Given that unigram surprisal also exhibits a moderate positive correlation with Node Count, there is a risk that the relationship between Node Count and PMI in Figure is merely an artifact of unigram surprisal.

To robustly partial out this confound, we fit Bayesian mixed-effects models that include unigram surprisal and word category as covariates. The Node Count effects remain credibly non-zero with the same signs (Appendix B), demonstrating that Node Count captures context richness independent of target-word frequency.
